title: Silent letters and liaison
goal: By the end of this lesson you can tell which final letters are silent, link words with liaison where French requires it, and avoid liaison where it is forbidden.

body: In French, a consonant at the end of a word is usually not pronounced. *petit*, *grand*, *trop*, *vous* and *Paris* all end in a silent letter.
A final *-e* without an accent is also silent: *table*, *porte*, *France*. Its job is often to make the consonant before it audible: *petit* (silent t) vs *petite* (t pronounced).
learn.tip: If the word ends in -e, the consonant before it is pronounced: grand / grande.

body: The final letters *c, r, f* and *l* are usually pronounced: *avec*, *bonjour*, *neuf*, *journal*. Remember them with the English word CaReFuL.
Big exception: verbs ending in *-er* and many nouns ending in *-er* keep the r silent: *parler*, *manger*, *le boulanger*.

Liaison happens when a normally silent final consonant is pronounced because the next word starts with a vowel or a silent *h*. The consonant moves to the start of the next word: *les amis* → [lay-za-mee].
Some letters change sound in liaison: *s* and *x* sound like [z], *d* sounds like [t], and *n* links as [n].

learn.h: When liaison is required, and when it is forbidden
body: Required: after articles and determiners (*les, des, un, mon, ces*), between a pronoun and its verb (*nous avons, ils ont*), after short adjectives before a noun (*petit ami*), and in fixed expressions (*tout à fait, de temps en temps*).
Forbidden: after *et* (*et / un*), before an aspirated *h* (*les / héros*, *les / haricots*), and after a singular noun (*un étudiant / anglais*).
Everything else is optional; casual speech, especially in Quebec, makes fewer optional liaisons.
learn.tip: Never link after et: 'et un' is always [ay uhn], never [ay-tuhn].

learn.h: Quebec: final t that comes back
body: In everyday Quebec speech, some final t's that are silent in standard French are pronounced: *tout* → [toutt], *lit* → [litt], *nuit* → [nuitt], *debout* → [deboutt].
Learn the standard silent form first for reading and writing, but expect to hear the t in Montreal and in the regions.

un‿étudiant [n], but no liaison after the singular noun étudiant

quebec.intro: In Quebec, some final t's that are silent in standard French are pronounced in everyday speech. You will hear 'toutt', 'litt' and 'nuitt' all the time.

items.note: y'é = il est in fast speech

drills.why: Final d is silent unless a liaison or an -e follows (grande).
Liaison: the s of les becomes [z] before a vowel.

drills.q: In which phrase is liaison forbidden?
drills.why: There is never a liaison after et.

drills.q: Which word keeps its final consonant sound?
drills.why: C is one of the CaReFuL letters that are usually pronounced.

drills.q: In 'un grand homme', the d is pronounced as…

drills.why: Héros starts with an aspirated h, so there is no liaison.

vocab.ex: Je suis debout à six heures.

pron.tip: puh-TEE vs puh-TEET: the -e makes the t audible.
Aspirated h, no liaison: lay / a-ree-KOH.
CaReFuL: the last sound is pronounced.

dialogue.fr: Bonjour! Vous êtes les nouveaux voisins?
dialogue.en: Hello! Are you the new neighbours?

dialogue.fr: Oui, deux enfants. Ils ont six ans et huit ans.
dialogue.en: Yes, two children. They are six and eight.

dialogue.fr: Mes enfants ont neuf ans. Ils vont être amis!
dialogue.en: My children are nine. They're going to be friends!

dialogue.fr: Bon, bonne soirée et bonne nuit!
dialogue.en: Well, have a good evening and good night!

questions.q: When did the neighbours move in?
How many children do the new neighbours have?
How old are speaker A's children?

speak.prompt: Read aloud, making every required liaison: 'Les enfants ont deux amis.'
Say how many children or friends you have, using 'J'ai … enfants / amis'.
speak.model: J'ai deux enfants et trois amis à Montréal.

speak.prompt: Say 'That's all, good night' the standard way, then the Quebec way.
speak.model: C'est tout, bonne nuit. / C'est toutt, bonne nuitt!

write.prompt: Write 4–5 sentences about your family or friends. Underline every liaison you would make when reading it aloud.
write.model: J'ai deux enfants. Mes enfants ont six ans et huit ans. Nous avons un petit chat. Mon ami habite à Laval. Il est très gentil.

quiz.q: Which final letters are usually pronounced (CaReFuL)?
quiz.why: C, R, F, L — remember CaReFuL.

quiz.q: Why is the r silent in 'parler'?
In liaison, s and x sound like…

quiz.why: Héros begins with an aspirated h.

options: The t is pronounced in petite
The p is silent in petite
quiz.why: The final -e makes the t audible.

quiz.q: How would many Quebecers say 'C'est tout'?
quiz.why: The final t is often pronounced in Quebec speech.
A pronoun and its verb are always linked: nous‿avons.
Before ans and heures, neuf sounds like [neuv].

quiz.q: Which word ends in a pronounced l?
quiz.why: Gentil, outil and fusil are exceptions with a silent l.
